title: #55 Hide Your Tell When Calling Upon Students to Explain Their Thinking
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton identifies a subtle bias in how teachers sequence which students they call on after a diagnostic question: consistently going to a correct-answer student first, or consistently saving the correct answer for last, unintentionally tips students off about whether they're right before anyone speaks. He argues this "tell" undermines the purpose of cold-calling, since a student who infers they're wrong may be reluctant to share reasoning, while a student who infers they're right may tune out of subsequent explanations. His solution is to remove the pattern: for multiple-choice diagnostic questions, always call on students in a fixed option order regardless of correctness, and for open-response questions, sweep systematically across the room in a set direction rather than by correctness. The result, he claims, is that students can no longer predict whether they're right from the order they're called on, which increases willingness to share reasoning and gives students an added incentive to keep listening throughout.
points: A consistent pattern of calling correct-answer students first (or last) is a "tell" that silently signals right/wrong to the class before any explanation is given.
Students who infer they're wrong from the calling order become reluctant to share their reasoning; students who infer they're right may disengage from listening to others.
The fix is procedural, not judgment-based: cycle through multiple-choice options in fixed order or sweep the room in a set spatial direction, irrespective of who is correct.
Removing the tell keeps all students uncertain of their own correctness until the discussion happens, which increases participation and sustains listening.
quotes: So, if you are a teacher who always goes to a student with the correct answer first, then anyone with a different answer immediately knows they are wrong and may not be willing to share their thinking when called upon.
Likewise, if you are a teacher who always saves the correct answer to last, anyone called upon first will know they are wrong and may also be reluctant to share their thoughts.

In both scenarios, there is also the issue of any student who has the correct answer immediately knowing they are correct and so tuning out of the explanations of students who have a different answer to them.
So, with a multiple-choice diagnostic question, I always pick a student who has chosen option A first, regardless if it is right or wrong, followed by B, then C, then D.

This simple technique means my students do not know whether they are right or wrong simply based on the order I choose them, so are more willing to share their reasoning, and have an extra incentive to keep listening.
